## Diagnostic routine

Start with an unseen, level-appropriate Listening set under the learner’s current test conditions. For each wrong answer, replay the relevant portion when practising, read the official key and available transcript, and record what happened: what was heard, what the question required, which answer was selected, and what evidence proves the correct answer. Look for a pattern across items or sets before assigning a cause.

The video describes six broad patterns. Use them as hypotheses to check, not exclusive student types:

1. **Repeated misses in one question family:** inspect whether the learner understands the instructions, follows the relevant discourse, and applies an appropriate method. Practise the weak family with worked examples and controlled sets, then transfer to a fresh timed set.
2. **Correct information heard, answer written incorrectly:** practise the actual error, such as spelling, singular/plural form, or word limits. Check whether the learner chose the right answer but lost a mark at answer entry.
3. **Errors clustered in Part 3:** review whether the learner lost speaker roles, contrast, agreement/disagreement, or the thread of a discussion. Part 3 is an educational conversation, usually with two main speakers; do not teach it as people necessarily talking over one another.
4. **Errors clustered in Part 4:** check the learner’s grasp of a sustained academic talk, its signposting, and key terms. Add focused listening and vocabulary work for relevant topics where the transcript confirms a language gap.
5. **Performance drops toward the end or on harder material:** test vocabulary, comprehension, task method, and attention separately. A location pattern alone does not prove that general English is the cause.
6. **Scattered misses or reported loss of focus:** compare the learner’s account with the recording and answer evidence. Build attention stamina progressively if sustained concentration is the problem; address unfamiliar words or task methods if the transcript shows those caused the errors.

Once a likely cause is supported by evidence, prescribe a small repair task: learn or rehearse the question method; drill an identified spelling pattern; listen to a short academic talk and map its structure; study a relevant word in context; or build concentration with gradually longer sessions. Then use unseen material to check transfer. Use broad podcasts, interviews, or lectures as extra exposure when they train a specific listening need, not as a replacement for IELTS-format practice.

## Official checks and limits

The IELTS Listening test has four parts and 40 questions, and candidates hear the recording once. Parts 1–2 cover everyday social situations; Part 3 is an educational conversation; Part 4 is an academic monologue. Each correct answer earns one mark, and raw-score-to-band conversions vary slightly by test version. The official practice page provides sample audio, answer keys, and transcripts for multiple question types. ([IELTS Listening format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-listening); [IELTS Listening sample tasks](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/sample-test-questions/academic-test); [IELTS scoring](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/your-results/ielts-scoring-in-detail))

- Use authentic material from official IELTS partners or other reliable publishers. The video’s suggestion that only Cambridge tests are valid, and that the strategy will not work on “fake” tests, is not established; official IELTS provides sample tasks with answer keys and transcripts.
- A timed baseline and error review are useful, but a few tests cannot guarantee a Band 9 or identify every language weakness. Treat the teacher’s claims about thousands of learners, quick score gains, and students rarely having a listening-skill problem as promotional, undocumented claims.
- The course offer, free fundamentals-course registration, discount, and success claims are marketing content, not listening instruction. ([9:04–11:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SYHWCn0GqCw&t=544s))

## Companion: diagnose a Listening plateau and build micro-listening

**Transcript:** [Get BAND 9 After Using These Listening Tips](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S_TVcsCFpTM), full English transcript in Glasp Reader through 31:36 of the 31:58 video; YouTube captions were unavailable.

**Chapter map:** [0:00–5:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S_TVcsCFpTM&t=0s) — two learners’ repeated Band 7 results and the need for diagnosis; [5:20–9:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S_TVcsCFpTM&t=320s) — timed baseline tests and a list of possible causes; [9:58–16:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S_TVcsCFpTM&t=598s) — analyze error locations, task families, connected speech, maps, and unknown vocabulary; [16:56–27:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S_TVcsCFpTM&t=1016s) — micro-listening and vocabulary learning; [27:16–31:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S_TVcsCFpTM&t=1636s) — question strategy promotion and slow-to-fast practice.

Use the lesson as a diagnostic extension to the six-pattern map above. Begin with a few unseen Listening tasks under realistic timing, then sort mistakes by section, task family, instruction-following, answer spelling, attention, vocabulary, accent familiarity, and difficulty separating connected speech. Look at the answer key and transcript for the specific missed passage; a score or section pattern alone does not identify the cause. One learner’s difficulty in Part 4 combined technical vocabulary with losing whole phrases in connected speech, while another’s map errors tracked a general difficulty with direction-finding. Treat both as individual cases and check the learner’s evidence before assigning practice.

For a connected-speech gap, choose a short, relevant clip from audio the learner wants to hear. Note a difficult phrase, then replay one sentence several times at a normal or reduced practice pace to notice how word boundaries and sounds connect. Check the transcript after a genuine attempt and replay again; do not keep guessing indefinitely. For an unknown word, first use the surrounding sentence or paragraph to make a possible meaning, then check a reliable dictionary. A word record can include meaning, pronunciation, a synonym where useful, and an example; review it later by recalling the meaning and using it in a new sentence. Link the practice to a stable daily routine, such as a commute or evening listening, but never ask a learner to read, type, or inspect notes while driving.

Separate skill practice from readiness checks. Slow, replayable work is for learning and diagnosis; fresh timed material checks whether the method transfers at the pace of the test. Question-family routines for multiple choice and maps should be taught from the dedicated lesson notes; this video identifies those as individual weaknesses but refers viewers to a downloadable resource instead of demonstrating the promised step-by-step routines. The advice to use only Cambridge books and to avoid booking a test until the instructor says so is not an official IELTS requirement. Several consistent results at the learner’s target level can inform readiness, but no practice score guarantees a future band. The Band 9 stories, guaranteed-readiness claim, and course promotion are unverified. ([official IELTS Listening sample tasks](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/sample-test-questions); [official Listening format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-listening))

## Companion: sort Listening errors before prescribing a strategy

**Transcript:** [The ONLY IELTS Listening Strategy You Need in 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gfTqr_9BMjs), English transcript from Glasp Reader reviewed through its final available caption at 12:08. YouTube captions were unavailable in the loaded exporter.

The lesson adds a useful first-pass diagnostic to the six-pattern map above. Begin with a fresh timed test (the instructor recommends two or three observations), then inspect errors by question family and answer entry, by part, and across the full test. Compare the answer key and transcript before deciding what skill to practise. These are possible patterns, not six fixed learner types:

- **Repeated misses in one question family:** teach and practise that task method with examples, then check transfer on unseen items.
- **The learner hears the answer but writes it incorrectly:** isolate spelling, word form, singular/plural, or answer-limit issues instead of re-teaching how to locate the information.
- **Part 3 errors:** investigate whether the learner can track speakers’ roles, positions, changes, and the discussion’s thread. IELTS describes Part 3 as an educational conversation between two main speakers; it need not contain people talking over each other.
- **Part 4 errors:** check vocabulary and comprehension in an academic monologue. Use a short lecture or talk for additional practice when the transcript confirms this need.
- **Errors increase in later parts:** test vocabulary, comprehension, task procedure, and sustained attention separately. The position of an error alone does not identify its cause.
- **Scattered errors or “I lost focus”:** use the recording and transcript to find missed words, unclear instructions, or a break in attention; build the implicated skill progressively.

For learners unfamiliar with multi-speaker discussion or academic talks, the teacher suggests relevant podcasts, programmes, radio, university lectures, and TED-style talks. Choose input that actually contains the needed language and interaction; use it as supplementary exposure alongside IELTS-style practice. A third-party 40/40 example, claims about thousands of Band 9 students and rapid score improvement, and the assertion that few learners have an underlying Listening problem are not independently established. The transcript shifts into course promotion before demonstrating the two promised learner cases, so this video contributes the diagnosis framework rather than new worked correction routines. ([0:00–4:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gfTqr_9BMjs&t=0s); [5:09–9:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gfTqr_9BMjs&t=309s); [11:41–12:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gfTqr_9BMjs&t=701s); [official IELTS Listening format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-listening))

## Companion learner review: diagnose a Listening plateau and practise focus

**Source:** [IELTS Advantage VIP Review: How I got a Band 9 in IELTS Listening](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rz_cjD8VPLs), `rz_cjD8VPLs`; full 17:32 English audio transcribed locally with faster-whisper large-v3-turbo because no usable caption track was available. The transcript is archived at `work/transcripts/rz_cjD8VPLs.asr.txt`; local ASR can mishear wording, so use the linked recording for exact phrasing.

Disha describes six test attempts, a Listening score plateau, inconsistent performance across modules, and anxiety before another test. She reports Listening 9, Reading 8, Writing 7, and Speaking 7; the scores and history are self-reported. She says she eventually stopped treating more practice tests as the answer by themselves and began inspecting what each wrong answer revealed. In her case she recalls plural/singular errors rather than spelling or grammar as the main Listening answer-entry issue. For course design, record a learner’s specific error and verify it against the key and transcript before choosing a repair; her account is an example, not a universal profile.

She recommends preparing by question type and making deliberate use of the short preview intervals between sections: identify what each question asks, notice likely answer forms, and keep the relevant question set in view. While listening, she says to follow the speaker’s meaning and connect ideas rather than attend only to isolated words; intonation and delivery may help interpret a speaker’s attitude or emphasis. Teach intonation as contextual evidence to combine with wording, not as a reliable shortcut for guessing an answer. If one answer is missed, recover attention for the next item instead of letting the loss cascade.

For a focus difficulty, Disha reports using meditation and a few deep breaths to return attention to the recording. Chris proposes building sustained attention gradually, in manageable increments, like increasing distance in a running plan. These are optional self-management practices; they do not replace diagnosis of unfamiliar vocabulary, task-method gaps, or comprehension problems. A practical routine is to identify the largest verified weakness, select one small daily exercise for it, and review whether performance improves on fresh material. Disha encourages learners not to give up and describes a friend’s call as a personal turning point. The practice process is useful to examine, but her results, course attribution, and immigration outcome are self-reported and do not establish a causal effect. The instructor’s advice not to book an exam until fully ready is a personal preparation recommendation, not an IELTS rule. The closing segment switches to the VIP waiting-list pitch and unsupported claims about course demand and success stories.
